title: Pixar Movie Ratings
text:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
pixar_films <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/pixar_films.csv')
public_response <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/public_response.csv')


pixarMovies <- merge(pixar_films, public_response, by = "film") |> select(1, 3:9) |> slice(1:10, 12:24)


#Highest rotten tomatoes Rating
high_rotten <- pixarMovies |> arrange(desc(rotten_tomatoes)) |> select(1,5) |>
  mutate(Movie = fct_reorder(film, rotten_tomatoes))

#Highest meta critic Rating
high_meta <- pixarMovies |> arrange(desc(metacritic)) |> select(1,6) |>
  mutate(Movie = fct_reorder(film, metacritic))
View(high_meta)

#Highest critics choice Rating
high_critic <- pixarMovies |> arrange(desc(critics_choice)) |> select(1,8) |> slice(1:21) |>
  mutate(Movie = fct_reorder(film, critics_choice))
View(high_critic)

#Introduction: This project analyzes Pixar film ratings using a combined data set of movie descriptions and public response metrics. Two data sets were merged to compare ratings across three platforms: Rotten Tomatoes, Metacritic, and Critics Choice. Rotten Tomatoes reports the percentage of positive reviews, Metacritic provides a weighted average critic score, and Critics Choice reflects ratings from professional film critics.The main variables of interest are film title, Rotten Tomatoes rating, Metacritic score, and Critics Choice rating. The data set includes 24 observations and 8 variables. The central question of this analysis is which Pixar films receive the highest overall ratings across these three platforms.
The data come from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository. Linked here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/readme.md
Some films are excluded due to missing ratings, such as Luca, which has no ratings available, and others lack Critics Choice scores which is Toy Story and A Bug’s Life. Meaning those two films were excluded in the Critic’s Choice graph. Additionally, the data set does not include all Pixar films, which should be considered when interpreting the results.
#Primary Visualizations
Rotten Tomatoes

ggplot(data = high_rotten, aes(x = Movie, y = rotten_tomatoes, fill = rotten_tomatoes)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(y = "Rotten Tomatoes Rating",
       title = "Rotten Tomatoes Rating for Pixar Movies") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal()








The Rotten Tomatoes visualization shows that Toy Story and Toy Story 2 share the highest rating, each receiving a perfect score of 100. An interesting pattern in this graph is that many films have identical or very similar ratings, making this distribution more compressed than the others. Compared to Metacritic and Critics Choice, Rotten Tomatoes shows the least variation among films, suggesting a generally strong love for Pixar movies.
Meta Critic

ggplot(data = high_meta, aes(x = Movie, y = metacritic, fill = metacritic)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(y = "Metacritic Rating",
       title = "Metacritic Rating for Pixar Movies") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal()








The Metacritic visualization reveals that Ratatouille has the highest Metacritic rating among the films analyzed. This result is interesting because Ratatouille falls closer to the middle of the distribution for both Rotten Tomatoes and Critics Choice ratings. Additionally, the Toy Story films rank lower on Metacritic than they do on the other two platforms, indicating differences in how each rating system evaluates the films.
Critics Choice

ggplot(data = high_critic, aes(x = Movie, y = critics_choice, fill = critics_choice)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    y = "Critic's Choice Rating",
    title = "Critic's Choice Rating for Pixar Movies") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_minimal()








The Critics Choice visualization indicates that Toy Story 2 holds the highest Critics Choice rating, with Toy Story 3 and Toy Story 4 also ranking within the top five. Although the original Toy Story does not have a Critics Choice rating in this data set, its strong performance in the other two rating systems suggests it likely would have scored highly here as well. Overall, this pattern highlights how well received the Toy Story franchise has been by critics and audiences.
#Conclusion and Wrap-Up One limitation of this analysis is the exclusion of certain films due to missing rating data. While these omissions were necessary to maintain accuracy in the visualizations, they reduce the overall sample size and may slightly limit the conclusions that can be drawn. Aside from this data exclusion, I don’t believe there are any other flaws with my approach. For future analysis I would explore whether film ratings influence the ratings. Another potential direction would be to examine movie runtimes and analyze whether Pixar films have generally increased in length over time of when the movie was released.
#Connection to Class Ideas These visualizations connect to class concepts by following best practices for effective data communication. The bar plots all start at zero, ensuring accurate visual comparison of ratings across films. Additionally, sequential color scales are used to represent low-to-high values, making it easier for viewers to interpret differences in ratings. Together, these design choices help clearly and effectively communicate patterns in the data.

title: The Bechdel Test
text:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)

movies <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-03-09/movies.csv')

bechdel <- movies |> mutate(result_binary = if_else(binary == "PASS", 1, 0)) |> select(1, 6, 24, 28, 35)

#Introduction:
The Bechdel Test, created by Alison Bechdel, is a measure of women representation in film and other forms of fiction to expose Hollywood’s gender bias. In order to pass the test the work must pass three criteria of having at least two named women that have a conversation with each other and that conversation can not be about a man. This basic criteria allows for the bare minimum amount of depth for female characters. This project looks at a data set movies from 1970 - 2013 of whether or not they pass the Bechdel test or not. The data set includes 1794 observations and 34 variables. The main variables of interest are film title, year of release, binary and IMDb rating. The central question of this analysis is how does the genre, imdb, and budget relate to a movie passing the Bechdel test and how has it change throughout the years.
The data come from the TidyTuesday GitHub repository. Linked here: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2021/2021-03-09/readme.md
It is important to note that some films have missing values for IMDb rating and genre. This should be considered when interpreting results for these two variables. The binary variable has also been changed to an indicator variable called ‘result_binary’ where 1 means the film passed the Bechdel test and 0 means the film failed the Bechdel test. This is to allow for easier interpretations.
#Primary Visualizations:

mean_bechdel <- bechdel |>
  group_by(result_binary) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rating = mean(imdb_rating, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = sd(imdb_rating, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n()))

ggplot(data = mean_bechdel, aes(x = factor(result_binary), y = mean_rating)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_rating - 2*se,
                    ymax = mean_rating + 2*se),
                width = 0.2) +
  labs(
    x = "Bechdel Test Result",
    y = "Mean IMDb Rating",
    title = "Mean IMDb Rating by Bechdel Result"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Fail", "Pass")) +
  theme_minimal()








This visualization shows that the average IMDb rating is higher for movies who do not pass the Bechdel Test versus movies that do. Although it looks like a big difference on the graph, the actual distance is around .27.

bechdel1 <- bechdel |>
  separate_rows(genre, sep = ", ") |>
  group_by(genre) |>
  summarise(prop_pass1 = mean(result_binary, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(prop_pass1)) |>
  mutate(genre = fct_reorder(genre, prop_pass1))

  ggplot(data = bechdel1, aes(x = genre, y = prop_pass1)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "Genre",
    y = "Proportion Passing Bechdel Test",
    title = "Bechdel Test Pass Rate by Genre"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme_minimal()








This barplot shows the proportion of movies that pass the Bechdel test based on their genre. It is important to note here that in this dataset, movies have multiple genres listed. To adjust for this, the dataset was tidied to count up each genre that is listed. Meaning that the sample size is larger than the other visualizations since one movie could represent 3 genres therefore placed in each genre in the count. The genre Music has the highest proportion of movies passing while Western has the least. When looking at the bottom of the barplot, the bottom five is crime, action, documentary, war, and western. This makes sense as those movies have usually been dominated by men.

time_bechdel <- bechdel |> 
  group_by(year) |> 
  summarise(prop_pass = mean(result_binary, na.rm = TRUE)) 

ggplot(data = time_bechdel, aes(x = year, y = prop_pass)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", 
       y = "Proportion Passing Bechdel Test",
    title = "Proportion of Films Passing the Bechdel Test Over Time") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme_minimal()








This line graph shows that throughout time (1970 - 2013) a higher proportion of movies made that year have passed the Bechdel test. Although it could and should get higher, this graph shows a positive indication the more female representation is occurring. It would be interesting to see movies form 2013-2025 and if the trend continues upward.
#Conclusion and Wrap-Up: One limitation of this analysis is the number of NA values in the IMBd rating and genre variable this may slightly limit the conclusions that can be drawn. I didn’t want to exclude those films to avoid tampering with the sample size for the final graph created. Another limitation could be that the number of movies each year is not the same. I don’t believe there are any other flaws with my approach. For future analysis I would explore how budget for the movie relates to passing the Bechdel test. I would also analyze whether there is a significant difference between passing the Bechdel test and gross earnings for the movie.
#Connection to Class Ideas: These visualizations connect to class concepts by practicing tidyverse skills and graphic designs. The first plot has error bars that we learned in class. For each of the graph I had to manipulate that dataset a bit to get the desired graphs for the variables I wanted. Together, these design aspects help clearly and effectively communicate patterns in the dataset and integrates class concepts.
